title: Atlantic Contact and the Columbian Exchange
description: European motives, transatlantic voyages, and the unequal consequences of biological and commercial exchange.
essential_question: Why did Atlantic contact transform Europe and the Americas so unevenly?
learning_objectives: Explain the economic and political motives for European exploration.
Trace major categories of exchange across the Atlantic.
Evaluate why disease and coerced labor had especially destructive effects in the Americas.

key_terms.definition: The transfer of plants, animals, diseases, people, and ideas between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres after 1492.
A Spanish labor system granting colonists claims to Indigenous labor and tribute.
The interconnected system linking Europe, Africa, and the Americas through migration, trade, conquest, and slavery.

presentation.tone: a teacher talking to a smart 16-year-old; plain, spoken, concrete

narration.text: [beat]The most important voyage in American history was a failure. In [date:1492], an Italian sailor named Christopher Columbus set out to find Asia. He never got there. He ran into a whole new world instead, and died believing he had reached the Indies. [beat] But his failure set off the largest exchange of people, plants, animals, and diseases the world had ever seen. And it was never equal.

narration.text: So why did anyone pay for the gamble? [beat] First, money. Europe craved Asia's spices and silks, but Italian city-states controlled the Mediterranean trade, and every middleman took a cut. A direct sea route would cut them out. [beat] Second, rivalry. Spain and Portugal were competing Catholic kingdoms, and new lands meant new power. In [date:1494], the Treaty of Tordesillas drew a line through the ocean and split the world between them. [beat] Third, faith. The Spanish crown wanted to spread Christianity, and its captains wanted glory. Wealth, rivalry, God. That was the fuel.

narration.text: In [date:1492], Columbus talked Spain's monarchs, Isabella and Ferdinand, into funding his westward bet. He argued the earth was smaller than the maps said. [beat] His three ships, the [es]Niña[/es], the [es]Pinta[/es], and the [es]Santa María[/es], made landfall after five weeks at sea. He called the island San Salvador and named the [es]Taíno[/es] people he met Indians, sure he had reached the Indies. The name stuck. Three more voyages followed, in [date:1493], [date:1498], and [date:1502], each one tightening Spain's grip. [beat] He kept a journal. On the very first day, he wrote this.

narration.text: Servants and converts, in the same breath. That tells you what Spain wanted. [beat] And the ships carried more than sailors. West across the Atlantic went sugar, wheat, and bananas, plus horses, cattle, goats, and chickens. The horse alone transformed Native cultures. [beat] East came corn, potatoes, sweet potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, and tobacco. New foods that helped feed a growing Europe. [beat] And crossing both ways, unseen: diseases, people, ideas. That is the Columbian Exchange.

narration.text: This is how Europe pictured the landing. [beat] Here is what the landing brought. Smallpox, influenza, measles. Diseases no one in the Americas had ever met. Between [date:1500] and [date:1650], somewhere between half and nine in ten Native people died. On Hispaniola, by one Spanish count, over a million [es]Taíno[/es] fell to a few hundred. [beat] The survivors faced the [es]encomienda[/es]: colonists granted the labor of Native communities, justified as protection and Christian teaching. In practice, mines and fields worked to death. [beat] Disease did what no army could.

narration.text: [beat]So Europe won the exchange. Not so fast. [beat] The silver and gold flooding into Spain set off runaway inflation. Taxes rose more than fivefold to pay for the empire's wars. Spain borrowed itself into debt. Ordinary Spaniards ended poorer, and did not recover for centuries. [beat] The exchange built an Atlantic World. But the gains flowed up, and the costs flowed down. Connected, not equal.
